guide.title: Sunnyside, Queens: Sunnyside Gardens, Queens Boulevard and the 7 Train
guide.intro: Sunnyside is a neighborhood in northwestern Queens and a standalone 2020 neighborhood tabulation area, QN0202, grouped for planning purposes under Long Island City-Sunnyside-Woodside, the approximation of Community District 2. It contains Sunnyside Gardens, designated a historic district by the Landmarks Preservation Commission under LP-2258 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 7, 1984 under reference number 84002919, roughly bounded by Queens Boulevard, 43rd and 52nd Streets, Barnett and Skillman Avenues. The commission's designation report calls it the first attempt to create a Garden City in the United States, and divides its buildings into twelve courts plus two Phipps Garden Apartment complexes, covering all or part of sixteen city blocks. Sunnyside Gardens Park lies inside that boundary, and the Flushing Line carries the 7 train to four stations within the neighborhood.

sections.heading: The garden city and its courts
sections.body:
Sunnyside Gardens is a designated New York City historic district, LP-2258, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 7, 1984 under reference number 84002919. The designated boundary runs easterly along the southern curbline of Barnett Avenue and southerly along the western curbline of 52nd Street, historically Dickson Street, to the southern curbline of 39th Avenue, historically Middleburg Avenue. The city's GIS boundary for the designated district measures about 54 acres.

The buildings, constructed between 1924-28, 1931-2 and 1935, are divided by the designation report into twelve courts — Carolin Gardens, Colonial Court, Hamilton Court, Hamilton Court Apartments, Harrison Place, Jefferson Court, Lincoln Court, Madison Court North and South, Monroe Court Apartments, Roosevelt Court, Washington Court and Wilson Court Apartments — and two Phipps Garden Apartment complexes, covering all or part of sixteen city blocks. The report calls Sunnyside Gardens "the first attempt to create a Garden City in the United States," and records that the City Housing Corporation purchased 76.67 acres of land in 1924, most from the Long Island Rail Road with smaller amounts from other landowners. In 1974 the New York City Planning Commission designated the area a "Special Planned Community Preservation District," one of four in the city.

Sunnyside Gardens Park, at 48-21 39th Avenue, was created as part of the original development and is included inside the designated district; the designation report calls it the largest privately held park in New York City and gives its size as about three acres. Celtic Park Apartments spans 42nd to 44th Streets between 48th and 50th Avenues, a nine-acre complex of 756 units converted to cooperative ownership in May 1986.

sections.heading: The name, the yard and Queens Boulevard
sections.body:
The local historian Vincent F. Seyfried records that Richard Bragaw built a gambrel-roofed house "in the English style atop Sunnyside Hill" in 1790, on the line of present-day 32nd Place between Northern Boulevard and Skillman Avenue, and that the house was demolished in July 1903 after the Pennsylvania Railroad acquired the property as part of the land assembly for the Sunnyside Yard. The Encyclopedia of New York City alternatively traces the modern neighborhood's name to a roadhouse built on Jackson Avenue in the 1850s and 1860s for visitors to the Fashion Race Course in Corona. The yard itself is split by the Department of City Planning into Sunnyside Yards (North), QN0161, which falls under the Astoria-Queensbridge community district equivalent, and Sunnyside Yards (South), QN0261, under the Long Island City-Sunnyside-Woodside approximation of Community District 2. A 2006 Landmarks Preservation Commission report on a Hunter's Point firehouse describes the historic city of Long Island City as "comprised of five separate neighborhoods: Ravenswood, Astoria, Steinway, Sunnyside, and Hunter's Point."

Along Queens Boulevard, a gantry carrying the neighborhood's name was erected at 46th Street in 1983. The Sunnyside Garden Arena stood at 44-11 Queens Boulevard, held about 2,500 spectators and operated until June 24, 1977; a portion of 45th Street was co-named in its honor in 2014. At 47-03 Queens Boulevard was the Coventry, a small live-music venue earlier called the Popcorn Pub: according to Ultimate Classic Rock and contemporaneous reporting, the rock band Kiss played its first concert there on January 30, 1973, and the Ramones also played early shows at the venue.

Thalia Spanish Theatre is at 41-17 Greenpoint Avenue, the Sunnyside branch of Queens Public Library at 43-06 Greenpoint Avenue, and Sunnyside Community Services at 43-31 39th Street. Sunnyside Shines is the business improvement district that carries the neighborhood's name. Sunnyside Reformed Church is at 48-03 Skillman Avenue, Mimar Sinan Mosque at 45-06 Skillman Avenue and Queen of Angels Church at 44-04 Skillman Avenue; The Episcopal Mission in Sunnyside is at 43-12 46th Street, the Sunnyside Muslim Center at 39-18 47th Avenue and Mosaic West Church at 46-01 43rd Avenue. The 45th St Composters and Community Garden, also known as Resistance is Fertile, is at 41-12 45th Street. The St. Pat's for All parade, founded in 2000 by Brendan Fay and Ellen Duncan, starts at 43rd Street and Skillman Avenue and its route continues into Woodside.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Four stations of the Flushing Line, served by the 7 train, stand inside the Sunnyside neighborhood tabulation area: 33 St-Rawson St, 40 St-Lowery St, 46 St-Bliss St and 52 St. MTA station records give all four an ADA value of 0. The nearest express stop is 61 St-Woodside, in Woodside, one stop beyond the neighborhood's easternmost station; the MTA record gives that station an ADA value of 1.

The "International Express" National Millennium Trail is described in its own designation as running from Sunnyside to Flushing, with Sunnyside as the named terminus.

faq.question: How do I get to Sunnyside?
faq.answer: By subway, the 7 train on the Flushing Line calls at four stations inside the Sunnyside neighborhood tabulation area: 33 St-Rawson St, 40 St-Lowery St, 46 St-Bliss St and 52 St. MTA station records give all four an ADA value of 0. The nearest express stop is 61 St-Woodside, in Woodside, one stop beyond the neighborhood's easternmost station, and the MTA record gives that station an ADA value of 1.

photos.title: The Sunnyside Arch over Queens Boulevard
photos.description: A steel gantry spans the roadway, its stepped tiers of curved bars rising above a blue sign reading SUNNYSIDE. Low storefronts flank the pavement on either side, a supermarket awning on the left and an optician and awninged shops on the right, with parked and moving cars and people crossing beneath the arch.
photos.author: Tdorante10

photos.title: Row houses in the Sunnyside Gardens Historic District
photos.description: An attached row of dark brick houses under steeply pitched slate roofs, the end unit gabled and set with dormer and attic windows. Trimmed hedges and low plantings screen the ground-floor bays from the sidewalk, mature plane trees shade the roadway, and cars are parked along both curbs.
photos.author: POLozito

places.name: Sunnyside Gardens Park
places.summary: A park of about three acres at 48-21 39th Avenue, created as part of the original Sunnyside Gardens development and included inside the Landmarks Preservation Commission's designated historic district. The designation report calls it the largest privately held park in New York City.

places.name: Phipps Garden Apartments
places.summary: Two apartment complexes on 39th Avenue at 50th Street, in Sunnyside, contributing property inside the Landmarks Preservation Commission's Sunnyside Gardens Historic District. The designation report counts them alongside the district's twelve courts.

photos.title: Phipps Garden Apartments from 39th Avenue
photos.description: A long brick apartment block with green-painted window frames, patterned brickwork panels and a stepped roofline. Raised lettering above the recessed central doorway reads PHIPPS GARDEN APARTMENTS. Bare plane trees, traffic signals and a 39 AV street sign stand at the curb under an overcast winter sky.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Celtic Park Apartments
places.summary: A nine-acre residential complex of 756 units spanning 42nd to 44th Streets between 48th and 50th Avenues, in Sunnyside. It was converted to cooperative ownership in May 1986.

places.name: Torsney Playground
places.summary: A NYC Parks playground at 41-15 Skillman Avenue, built in the 1950s and named for George F. Torsney, a local political figure and World War I veteran. The park contains the Lou Lodati Playground.
places.history: The Lou Lodati Playground was named in 1999 by New York City Council resolution for the longtime community organizer Lou Lodati (1908–1996), known locally as "the Mayor of Sunnyside." NYC Parks gives both the park's sign name and its 311 name as Torsney Playground, and its sign text describes the park as serving the Sunnyside area.

places.name: L/CPL Thomas P. Noonan Jr. Playground
places.summary: A NYC Parks playground at 42-01 Greenpoint Avenue, in Sunnyside. NYC Parks records the property under two ZIP codes, 11104 and 11377.

places.name: Lt. Michael R. Davidson Playground
places.summary: A NYC Parks playground at 50-02 39th Avenue, in Sunnyside.

places.name: Sabba Park
places.summary: A NYC Parks property in Sunnyside, on Queens Boulevard between 48th Street, Greenpoint Avenue and 50th Street.

places.name: Thalia Spanish Theatre
places.summary: A theatre at 41-17 Greenpoint Avenue. Its own site counts over 255 world and American premieres and 252 awards.

places.name: Sunnyside Community Services
places.summary: A community organization at 43-31 39th Street. Its own site says it serves over 16,000 people.

places.name: Queens Public Library, Sunnyside
places.summary: The Sunnyside branch of Queens Public Library, at 43-06 Greenpoint Avenue.
places.history: Queens Public Library prints the branch's address with the mailing designation "Long Island City, NY 11104"; the Department of City Planning's address database gives Sunnyside as the locality for the same address.

places.name: Sunnyside Arch
places.summary: A gantry over Queens Boulevard at 46th Street, carrying the neighborhood's name. It was erected in 1983.

places.name: Sunnyside Garden Arena
places.summary: The former Sunnyside Garden Arena, at 44-11 Queens Boulevard. It held about 2,500 spectators and operated until June 24, 1977.
places.history: A portion of 45th Street was co-named in the arena's honor in 2014.

places.name: The Coventry
places.summary: A former small live-music venue at 47-03 Queens Boulevard near 47th Street, earlier called the Popcorn Pub.
places.history: According to Ultimate Classic Rock and contemporaneous reporting, the rock band Kiss played its first concert at the Coventry on January 30, 1973; the Ramones also played early shows at the venue.

places.name: Sunnyside Reformed Church
places.summary: A church at 48-03 Skillman Avenue, in Sunnyside.
places.history: The local historian Vincent F. Seyfried, in 300 Years of Long Island City, 1630–1930 (1984), records the congregation as organized in July 1896.

places.name: 45th St Composters and Community Garden
places.summary: A community garden at 41-12 45th Street, also known as Resistance is Fertile.
